One-sentence judgment: a Communications Teacher, Postsecondary is not just being able to lecture, but teaching communications courses at a college or university (such as organizational communication, public relations, broadcasting, and journalism) while completing course design, grading, academic research, and service to students and the department; O*NET defines this occupation as teaching communications courses such as organizational communication, public relations, broadcasting, and journalism; it includes teachers who are primarily teaching and teachers who combine teaching and research; this page follows the O*NET-SOC 25-1122.00 precise occupational basis.

The work of a Communications Teacher, Postsecondary can be divided into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is teaching and courses and assessment: prepare course materials such as syllabi, assignments, and handouts; prepare for and teach undergraduate or graduate courses on topics such as public speaking, media criticism, and oral tradition; initiate, lead, and moderate classroom discussions; read and grade student assignments, course papers, and examinations; compile and administer examinations or assign that work to others; plan, evaluate, and revise course offerings, course content, course materials, and teaching methods; select and obtain materials and supplies such as textbooks; and maintain student attendance, grade, and other required records. The second is research and academic output: conduct research in a specific field of knowledge and publish results in professional journals, books, or electronic media; keep up with developments and technological advances in the communications field by reading current literature, talking with colleagues, and attending professional conferences; write grant proposals to obtain external research funding; compile bibliographies of professional materials for outside reading assignments; and collaborate with colleagues on teaching and research issues. The third is academic advising and departmental and public service: advise undergraduate or graduate students on teaching, internships, and research work; advise students on academic and vocational curricula and career issues; maintain regular office hours to advise and assist students; serve as faculty advisor to student organizations; take part in student recruitment, registration, and placement activities; serve on academic or administrative committees dealing with institutional policy, departmental affairs, and academic matters; take on administrative duties such as department chair; take part in campus and community events; and provide professional consulting services to government or industry. This occupation includes both teaching-focused and combined teaching and research roles; research, funding, committee, or department chair tasks follow the actual appointment duties, and all 23 tasks are not written as mandatory for every position every semester. Course, grade, enrollment, research, and external commitment authorities are verified separately per the applicable systems, and teachers are not uniformly treated as degree or departmental approvers.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether course objectives align with the program and assessment standards; whether assignment and examination grading is reproducible and can withstand review; whether citation and data and research authorship comply with academic integrity standards; whether generative AI use is within the permitted course and institutional scope and truthfully declared; whether student grades and privacy and psychological and safety situations are handled per the system; and whether teaching and research records and materials archiving are traceable.
Judgment one: whether course objectives align with the program and assessment standards

Align course objectives, program requirements, and assessment methods, and write the grading standards and assignment requirements clearly and explain them to students before the course begins; when course content or assessment methods need to change, revise them per departmental procedures and keep a version record, and do not substitute temporary standards for a published plan.
Judgment two: whether assignment and examination grading is reproducible and can withstand review

Grade per uniform standards and keep the grading basis and samples; review grade disputes per institutional procedures, proactively correct discovered grading errors and record them, and do not change published grading standards because of student appeals or personal relationships.
Judgment three: whether citation and data and research authorship comply with academic integrity standards

Handle citation, data, authorship, and conflicts of interest per disciplinary standards and institutional systems; confirm author order and data use authorization before submission and collaboration; do not use materials that cannot be verified, and document the verification process.
Judgment four: whether generative AI use is within the permitted scope and truthfully declared

First confirm the course, institutional, and journal rules on generative AI use: within the permitted scope it may be used for material organization and language polishing, but it must not replace your own responsibility for research conclusions, assessment judgments, and academic views; declare the tool and purpose as required and keep verifiable original materials.
Judgment five: whether student grades and privacy and psychological and safety situations are handled per the system

Manage student records and referral procedures per the actual authorization, and do not upload them to unauthorized tools or channels. US FERPA/34CFR99 covers institutions receiving Department of Education program funds under 99.1 (including eligible student financial aid and institutional components); 99.3 education records must be directly related to a student and maintained by the institution or a party acting for it, with exclusions such as sole possession memory; 99.30 generally requires dated signed written consent, and 99.31 has exceptions for school officials with a legitimate educational interest and qualifying controlled outsourcing, so not all information is prohibited from transmission and not every tool is permitted. 99.36 emergency disclosure for health and safety must be necessary and involve an articulable significant threat, with corresponding records under 99.32; not all psychological risk can be disclosed unconditionally, and teachers are not granted clinical judgment authority. China and other jurisdictions are verified separately for applicable regulations and institutional processes.
Judgment six: whether teaching and research records and materials archiving are traceable

Archive syllabus and material versions, assignment and examination and grading records, research data and manuscript versions, and advising and office hours and service records per institutional requirements and assign them to a person and time, so that the teaching and research process can be reviewed by others rather than leaving only a verbal account.

paragraphs: The six directions share part of their abilities with this occupation: disciplinary knowledge, writing and expression, literature and research literacy, and awareness of assessment standards and norms. The real difference lies in the object and the responsibility: the language and literature, education, and sociology directions are also college teaching but with different disciplines and courses; the journalism and public relations directions deliver works and proposals to the public or organizations and do not carry course design and grading responsibility; the broadcast technician direction focuses on technical and equipment support; and this occupation simultaneously carries course design, lecturing, and grading in the college classroom plus academic research and departmental service responsibilities. When choosing, it is suggested to first verify with a deliverable syllabus, assessment plan, and research and writing plan exercise, rather than comparing names first.

The comparison basis is the occupational definition and task and work activity and work context description on the O*NET-SOC 25-1122.00 page, the related and adjacent occupation codes listed on that page, the adjacent occupation slug list registered by this evidence route, and the public occupational materials of each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial summary and does not constitute a teaching qualification, appointment, professional title, degree, or legal conclusion.

The table below compares the positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: English Language and Literature Teachers, Postsecondary; Education Teachers, Postsecondary; Sociology Teachers, Postsecondary; News Analysts, Reporters, and Journalists; Public Relations Specialists; and Broadcast Technicians. The four columns answer the same kind of question: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choose it.

College English language and literature teachers focus on language and literature courses and research, and their research object is language, literature, and writing; this occupation's courses and research center on the fields of communication and media and journalism and public expression.

People willing to study language and literary texts over the long term are suited to that direction; people willing to study communication processes and media and public expression are suited to this occupation.
Mainly language and literature courses and papers and monographs.
English Language and Literature Teachers, Postsecondary

Education Teachers, Postsecondary focus on education theory, curriculum and instruction, and teacher preparation courses, and their research object is educational systems and learning processes; this occupation focuses on communications courses and research.
People willing to study educational systems and instructional design are suited to that direction; people willing to study communication and media and journalism are suited to this occupation.
Mainly education courses and education research papers.
Education Teachers, Postsecondary

College sociology teachers focus on sociology theory and research methods courses, and their research object is social structure and group behavior; this occupation takes communication phenomena and media and public communication as its object.
People willing to research social structure and group behavior are suited to that direction; people willing to research communication and media and public opinion are suited to this occupation.
Mainly sociology courses and empirical research papers.
Sociology Teachers, Postsecondary

News Analysts, Reporters, and Journalists work at gathering, writing, and reporting and news analysis and produce news works for the public, and usually do not carry course design and grading responsibility; this occupation focuses on courses, assessment, and academic research in the college classroom.

People willing to do frontline reporting and writing and publish to the public are suited to that direction; people willing to turn communications practice into courses and research are suited to this occupation.
Mainly news works and reports and commentary.
News Analysts, Reporters, and Journalists

Public Relations Specialists work at organizational external communication, media relations, and reputation maintenance, delivering communication proposals per organizational goals; this occupation teaches and researches and is responsible for courses and assessment.

People willing to do external communication and relationship maintenance in an organization are suited to that direction; people willing to do course design and research in higher education are suited to this occupation.
Mainly communication proposals, media relations, and reputation reports.
Public Relations Specialists

Broadcast Technicians focus on the technical support of broadcast systems and audio and video equipment and do not carry course lecturing and academic assessment; this occupation focuses on content and teaching and research.

People willing to do broadcast and audio and video technical support are suited to that direction; people willing to work on communications content and teaching and research are suited to this occupation.
Mainly broadcast and equipment and signal support records.
Broadcast Technicians

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires adding new abilities and qualifications: the other college teaching directions require doctoral or master's training in the corresponding discipline and the corresponding course and research experience; the journalism direction requires frontline reporting and writing works and journalism practice training; the public relations direction requires organizational communication and media relations and communication proposal design experience; the broadcast technology direction requires technical training and equipment experience in audio and video and broadcast systems. Writing and expression, research methods, and normative awareness are transferable, but the disciplinary admission and responsibility boundaries of each direction must be re-established.

Automatically generated course materials or literature summaries may contain incorrect citations or statements inconsistent with disciplinary consensus; adopting them without verifying the original literature and data increases teaching and academic risk.

Distinguish student education records, personal information, unpublished research, and contract materials per the actual authorization, and do not write all research materials as FERPA records. US FERPA/34CFR99 covers institutions receiving Department of Education program funds under 99.1 (including eligible student financial aid and institutional components); 99.3 education records must be directly related to a student and maintained by the institution or a party acting for it, with exclusions such as sole possession memory; 99.30 generally requires dated signed written consent, and 99.31 has exceptions for school officials with a legitimate educational interest and qualifying controlled outsourcing, so not all information is prohibited from transmission and not every tool is permitted. 99.36 emergency disclosure for health and safety must be necessary and involve an articulable significant threat, with corresponding records under 99.32; not all psychological risk can be disclosed unconditionally, and teachers are not granted clinical judgment authority. China and other jurisdictions are verified separately for applicable regulations and institutional processes.

Editorial version risk scenario: when the tool or model version and the input material version are not recorded, it may hinder reproducing assisted grading or research drafts; this is not evidence of tool accuracy.

Drawing a judgment directly from automatically aggregated teaching data or literature conclusions may hide differences in sample, scope, and applicable conditions.

Write the data source and time and scope and the person who performed it clearly, label the scope of application of the conclusion, keep the original records, and leave assessment and academic conclusions to positions with the corresponding authority to confirm.

entries.answer: Daily work is mainly teaching and courses and assessment, research and academic output, and academic advising and departmental and public service: preparing course materials such as syllabi, assignments, and handouts; preparing for and teaching undergraduate or graduate courses on topics such as public speaking and media criticism and oral tradition; initiating and leading and moderating classroom discussions; reading and grading student assignments and course papers and examinations; compiling and administering examinations or assigning them to others; planning, evaluating, and revising course offerings and content and methods; conducting research in a specific field of knowledge and publishing results in professional journals, books, and electronic media; keeping up with developments in the communications field by reading literature and attending conferences; writing grant proposals; advising undergraduate or graduate students on teaching, internships, and research work; advising on academic and career issues and maintaining regular office hours; and serving on academic or administrative committees and taking part in admissions and placement and campus and community activities. O*NET work context shows 92% use email every day, 65% have face-to-face discussions every day, 58% have continuous contact with others, 74% work more than 40 hours per week, and 50% need public speaking more than once a week.
entries.question: What does a Communications Teacher, Postsecondary do every day?

entries.answer: College English language and literature teachers, education teachers (postsecondary), and college sociology teachers are all college teachers, but the disciplinary object and course system differ; news analysts, reporters, and journalists work at gathering and writing and reporting and news analysis and usually do not carry course and grade determination responsibility; public relations specialists work at organizational external communication and relationship maintenance; broadcast technicians focus on broadcast and audio and video technical support; graduate teaching assistants focus on assisting teaching and grading and leading discussion sections; instructional coordinators focus on course and teaching project coordination; this occupation centers on course design, lecturing, and grade determination in the college classroom plus academic research and departmental service. Shared abilities do not mean interchangeability: the disciplinary admission, appointment form, and responsibility boundaries differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer: That cannot be inferred. The core tasks of this occupation include course design and lecturing and assessment, academic research and writing, and academic advising and departmental service; judging whether students have met course objectives, judging whether research data and conclusions hold up, and being responsible for course quality and academic integrity all require disciplinary training and institutional authorization and acceptance of responsibility. In addition, the ILO report registered by this evidence route discusses what exposure indicators can and cannot answer, not a replacement rate or job loss projection. The more reliable tool uses are course materials and literature and language and record drafts.

entries.answer: Judging from the task structure, the earlier-affected parts are the structurable and digitizable steps: course material and example organization, literature review and format organization, language polishing, teaching data and assignment feedback drafts, and record and file aggregation. The later-affected parts are the steps that need judgment and responsibility: grade determination and academic judgment, research questions and conclusions, live classroom interaction and academic advising, and handling student privacy and psychological and safety situations. It must be emphasized that this judgment is an editorial summary, not an exposure measure or position projection provided by a source.
entries.question: Which tasks are most easily assisted?

entries.answer: Judging students' level of understanding in the live classroom and adjusting immediately, raising valuable research questions and judging whether data and conclusions hold up, identifying risk signals in academic advising and referring per the system, and taking responsibility in grade and academic and student affairs matters. These abilities depend on disciplinary training and institutional authorization; replacing any of these steps with tool output makes it impossible to answer who is responsible for course quality and academic integrity.

subject.summary: Teaches communications courses in higher education, such as organizational communication, public relations, broadcasting, and journalism; includes teachers who are primarily teaching and teachers who combine teaching and research: preparing course materials such as syllabi and assignments and handouts; preparing for and teaching and moderating classroom discussion on topics such as public speaking and media criticism and oral tradition; reading and grading student assignments and course papers and examinations; compiling and administering examinations or assigning them to others; planning, evaluating, and revising course offerings and course content and teaching methods; conducting research in a specific field of knowledge and publishing results in professional journals and books and electronic media; keeping up with developments in the communications field by reading literature and attending conferences and writing grant proposals; advising undergraduate or graduate students on teaching and internships and research work and maintaining regular office hours to provide academic and career advice; serving on academic or administrative committees and taking part in admissions and placement and campus and community activities; and providing professional consulting services to government or industry.
